note: Anyone can paste a product name into a chatbot and get a tidy summary. These aren't that. Each one has a point of view you can argue with, evidence from using the thing myself, an estimate with its assumptions on show, and a bet I'd defend in a room. Flip "Show red pen" on any teardown to see why each part is built the way it is.

items.title: The disposable route
items.card: Why I reach for directions, not navigation, on Indian roads — and the one change that fixes it.
items.thesis: Google Maps treats every route as disposable. It recomputes after a missed turn, and in directions mode after every unlock, rather than holding the route you committed to. On Indian roads most misses are cheaply recoverable — but only if the product tells you before it quietly moves you.

thesisPen.note: One line, and you can disagree with it. It targets a design choice — recompute vs hold — not a vague "navigation is bad".

pen.note: The job is in the driver's words, and it names the constraint that matters: while I can still fix it cheaply.

blocks: A car driver on a long drive, or a half-familiar city route — phone mounted or in a pocket, not running full navigation the whole way.

blocks.callout: The job: keep me on the route I started on, and tell me the instant I'm off it — while I can still fix it cheaply.

list: The few seconds after a missed turn.
A glance every 5–10 km on a long drive.

sections.h: Business model & the metric that matters

pen.note: Says how the product earns before proposing changes, and the estimate shows its assumptions instead of a made-up number.

blocks: Maps earns through local search, ads and the Maps Platform — not navigation directly. Navigation earns its keep as the habit that keeps bringing people back.

list: North star (for this teardown): trips completed with Maps in use, without the driver abandoning it.
Bet metric: minutes of detour per missed turn — today vs with an instant alert.
Guardrails: screen taps per trip (safety); false alerts on deliberate deviations.

blocks.sub: The estimate — first-principles, every assumption on show

list: Per incident (one data point, the drive below): a silent recompute baked in ~90 min; an alert at the fork recovers in ~2 min → ~88 min saved.

Per affected driver / year: ~6 long unfamiliar drives with a recoverable miss × ~25 min average silent detour (conservative vs the 90 above) against ~3 min with an alert → ~22 min per incident, ~2+ hours a year.
Scale: × the number of affected drivers — left as a multiplier, since I won't invent India's driver count.

blocks: The point is a method with its assumptions visible, not a fabricated crore figure.

pen.note: Both moments are first-hand — one of them quantified. Not a screen-by-screen tour.

num.body: On an 11-hour interstate drive with several route options, passing through a small town, I missed the turn for a flyover. Maps recomputed silently. I noticed about 20 minutes into the new route — by which point turning back meant losing roughly 40 minutes. The trip finished at 12:30, about 1.5 hours (≈14%) over the 11-hour route. Flagged at the fork, recovery would have been about 2 minutes.

num.lead: The unlock on a long drive.
num.body: In directions mode the screen sleeps. Each time I unlock, it refreshes the directions and can show a different route from the one I started on. All I wanted was a check every 5–10 km — instead the route wouldn't hold still.

pen.note: Credits the competing features and names exactly which half each one solves, instead of hiding them.

list: Asking before a traffic reroute. For traffic, Maps surfaces a faster route and lets you choose — the driver stays in charge. The bet simply extends this to missed turns.

Flyover callouts (40 cities, 2024) and AI narrow-road avoidance. Google diagnosed the flyover-vs-service-road moment correctly — but solved the warning (a flyover is coming), not the recovery (when you miss it). Half the moment.

Glanceable directions (2023–24): lock-screen ETA and next turn without starting navigation. Not on my phone; where it exists it's off by default and still auto-updates the route on a detour. Solves the screen, not the route.

pen.note: Ranked by impact, with the reason #1 hurts (the silence) named, and the data problem pushed down openly.

num.body: Highest impact: the recovery window is spent before the driver knows it exists. The silence, not the reroute itself, is what makes a disposable route cost you.

num.lead: Unlock refresh with no held route.
num.body: The route won't hold still between glances.

num.lead: Road data that doesn't match the road.
num.body: Real, but a data problem that's already being worked on — ranked below the two design problems.

pen.note: Answers "why haven't they done it?" before you ask, and names the one mechanism the bet rests on — alert speed, not manual rerouting.

rows: Pick a route; it's held unless you change it
Instant voice alert at the fork, both costs shown: "Loop back: +2 min. Continue: +1 h 30 min." Picks the faster option itself after ~5 s
Lock screen: "On route ✓ · next decision in 12 km", against the held route
Optional spoken check-in every N km

list: Core of the bet: hold the route, and alert fast enough to recover cheaply. The value is flagging the deviation while recovery is still cheap — not manual rerouting.
Trade-off: more prompts mid-drive, and the risk of nagging on deliberate deviations. Mitigation: voice only, a safe default, suppressed once the deviation rejoins the route.

Why haven't they done it? One global routing logic; a silent reroute still "succeeds" on the dashboard (you still arrive); glanceable being off by default hints Google doubts the middle mode is wanted.

pen.note: Names the data and the failure mode that would kill the bet.

list: Google's data may show most deviations are deliberate — then auto-reroute is right for most drivers, and this should be opt-in.
An instant alert at every fork could become noise in dense city driving — the opposite failure to silence.
A held route can go stale (a closure, an accident). "Committed" must never mean blind, so the traffic prompt stays.

dropToPm.why: A complaint, not a claim. Nothing to test.
Misses that silent recomputation — not rerouting as such — spends the recovery window.

dropToPm.weak: "Fix the route; any deviation sounds an alarm and asks permission to reroute."
dropToPm.why: Asks the driver to look and tap at the most stressful moment, fires on every deliberate cut, and by the time you'd tap, recovery is already expensive.

dropToPm.weak: No mention of flyover callouts or glanceable directions.
dropToPm.why: A Maps PM stops reading there.
